emergencyNumber: 999 (emergency — ambulance, police, fire), 111 (NHS 111 medical helpline for non-emergencies)
healthcareSystem: Universal (National Health Service / NHS — tax-funded, free at point of use for all)
qualityNotes: World-class healthcare with the NHS. Emergency treatment is free for everyone. English is universal. Wait times for non-emergency care can be long. Pharmacies can treat minor ailments under the Pharmacy First scheme.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-5:30pm weekdays, reduced hours on weekends. Many major chains (Boots, Superdrug) have late-night or 24/7 locations in cities.
pharmacyTips: Pharmacies are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. Under 'Pharmacy First,' pharmacists can treat certain conditions and prescribe specific medications without a GP appointment. Boots and Superdrug are the main chains.
prescriptionRules: Prescriptions from NHS doctors are accepted. Private prescriptions from other countries require validation by a UK doctor. Many common medications require prescriptions here that are OTC in other countries.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products are available OTC in limited quantities (max 8 days supply) but may require pharmacist consultation. Larger quantities require a prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Vyvanse, methylphenidate/Ritalin)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A UK prescription is required. Bring documentation from your doctor. NHS has strict prescribing guidelines for ADHD medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium/diazepam, Xanax/alprazolam)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. UK has strict guidelines. Only small quantities for personal use may be allowed with a doctor's letter.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis was legalized in 2018 but is only prescribed by specialist doctors for specific conditions (rare pediatric epilepsy, MS spasticity, chemotherapy-induced nausea). Most tourists cannot access it.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter and prescription for all medications. Bring medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry a letter from your prescribing doctor in English. Consider registering with a GP if staying 6+ months.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not required, but strongly recommended for non-emergency care, repatriation, and specialist treatment.
travelInsurance.tips: Emergency care (A&E/ER) is free for all at NHS hospitals. However, if you're admitted for non-emergency treatment, you'll need travel insurance. The UK has no reciprocal healthcare agreement with the US, so Americans pay for all non-emergency NHS care.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for close contact with locals)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccines are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the UK.
foodSafetyTips: The UK has excellent food safety standards. Restaurant and pub food is generally very safe. Watch out for high salt content in some processed foods. Shellfish and raw oysters from reputable establishments are safe.
medicalTourismNote: The UK offers world-class medical care for international patients, particularly in London. Costs are higher than some destinations but quality is excellent.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to the United Kingdom. Emergency numbers (999, 111), pharmacy tips, NHS healthcare overview, restricted medications, and travel insurance advice.
